title: Unapproved assets are both prohibited and priced at a 100% haircut so the margin engine survives an enumeration failure
content:
A.6.1.1.1.3.7.2.2.6 does two things that look redundant: "Exposure to unapproved assets and/or futures products **is not permitted**, and incurs a collateral haircut rating of **+100% / −100%**. Long and short exposure to unapproved products will not be counted as offsetting each other. Frequent or significant exposure to unapproved assets or products may result in recall of the loan amount or liquidation of outstanding positions."

If something is forbidden, why also price it? Because a whitelist is a claim about the world that will eventually be wrong. New tokens appear, a wrapped version diverges from its approved form, a DEX pool quietly adds an unlisted asset, an exchange lists a product mid-position. A rule that only prohibits fails silently at exactly those moments: the position exists, and the margin engine has no number for it.

Assigning 100% makes the fallback safe rather than undefined. An unapproved holding contributes zero to stressed portfolio value, so the account's health immediately reflects the position as a total loss and margin requirements respond automatically — no human needs to notice first. The no-offsetting clause closes the obvious exploit of pairing two unapproved positions to net to nothing.

The layered response then escalates by *pattern* rather than by instance. A single accidental exposure is absorbed by the haircut; "frequent or significant" exposure triggers recall or liquidation, which is a judgment about the borrower rather than the position.

The same defence-in-depth appears in the DEX rule at A.6.1.1.1.3.7.2.2.5: a pool failing any approval condition "is treated as an unapproved asset/product" — routed into this 100% bucket rather than into an error. Prohibition states the intent; the haircut is what holds when the intent is violated.
description: Exposure to unapproved assets is not permitted, yet still carries a +100%/−100% rating with no long/short offsetting, and repeated use can trigger loan recall or liquidation.
